params.question: Haemolytic anaemia develops whenever red blood cells are destroyed before their normal 120-day lifespan.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Haemolysis is premature red cell destruction, but haemolytic anaemia occurs only when destruction outpaces the bone marrow's compensatory capacity (6–8× baseline). In a compensated haemolytic state, haemolysis is present but haemoglobin remains near normal because the marrow keeps pace.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Haemolysis is the premature destruction of red cells, but haemolytic anaemia develops only when that destruction outpaces bone marrow compensation. The marrow can increase output 6–8 times its baseline. When destruction stays within this reserve, the patient has a compensated haemolytic state — haemolysis without anaemia.

interactions.label: A patient presents with jaundice but has normal-coloured urine and normal stools

params.question: A patient presents with jaundice but has normal-coloured urine and normal stools. Which type of jaundice does this pattern indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In obstructive jaundice, conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood and spills into the urine (dark urine), while absence of bile in the intestine produces pale clay-coloured stools — the opposite of this pattern.
Hepatocellular jaundice produces a mixed picture with both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin elevated. Urine may darken due to conjugated bilirubin excretion, unlike the normal urine seen here.

Correct. This is acholuric jaundice. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which is albumin-bound and cannot be filtered by the kidneys. Bilirubin still reaches the liver and gut normally, so stool colour is preserved.

Neonatal jaundice is also unconjugated but has specific causes (immature hepatic conjugation, increased red cell turnover at birth). In an adult, this pattern of normal urine and normal stools with jaundice points to pre-hepatic haemolytic jaundice.

overallFeedback.feedback: Normal-coloured urine and stools with jaundice points to pre-hepatic haemolytic jaundice. This is called acholuric jaundice. The unconjugated bilirubin from red cell breakdown is albumin-bound and does not spill into the urine.
Jaundice with normal urine and normal stools is called acholuric jaundice — the hallmark of pre-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice caused by elevated unconjugated bilirubin.

params.question: Which laboratory finding most reliably distinguishes sickle cell disease from beta-thalassaemia major?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia major have elevated reticulocytes due to chronic haemolysis and compensatory erythropoiesis. This finding is shared and does not discriminate between them.

answers.text: Presence of target cells on the peripheral smear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Target cells appear in both conditions — alongside sickle cells in SCD and alongside microcytic hypochromic cells in thalassaemia. They do not help distinguish the two.

Correct. In sickle cell disease, the MCV is normal (normocytic anaemia). In beta-thalassaemia, impaired globin chain synthesis produces microcytic hypochromic red cells with a low MCV. This single finding separates the two.
Haemoglobin F is elevated in both conditions — above 90% in beta-thalassaemia major and variably raised in homozygous sickle cell disease. It does not reliably distinguish between them.

overallFeedback.feedback: Sickle cell disease produces a normocytic anaemia (normal MCV), while beta-thalassaemia produces microcytic hypochromic red cells with a low MCV. This is the single most reliable feature separating the two conditions.
The MCV is normal in sickle cell disease but low in thalassaemia. This single finding is the most reliable initial discriminator between the two haemoglobinopathies.

interactions.label: Why should glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity be measured after an acute

params.question: Why should glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity be measured after an acute haemolytic crisis has resolved, rather than during it?

answers.text: The oxidant stress during a crisis artificially degrades the enzyme in the blood sample

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: G6PD is measured in a blood sample under controlled laboratory conditions. In vivo oxidant stress does not degrade the enzyme in vitro — the issue is which cell population dominates the sample.

answers.text: Reticulocytes carry higher G6PD levels and produce falsely normal results during a crisis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. During a crisis, the oldest G6PD-deficient cells have already been destroyed. The circulating blood is enriched with young reticulocytes that carry near-normal enzyme activity, masking the underlying deficiency.

answers.text: Concurrent infection suppresses hepatic synthesis of G6PD

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: G6PD is an intracellular enzyme synthesised within red cell precursors in the bone marrow, not by the liver. Its measurable activity reflects the age profile of the circulating red cell population.

answers.text: Haemoglobinuria from the crisis interferes with the spectrophotometric assay

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The G6PD assay is performed on washed red cells or a haemolysate, not on plasma or urine. Free haemoglobin in plasma does not interfere with the enzyme measurement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Reticulocytes (young red cells released during the compensatory marrow response) carry higher G6PD levels than mature cells. Since the deficient older cells have already been destroyed, the sample is enriched with reticulocytes, masking the true deficiency.

During a crisis, the G6PD-deficient older cells have been destroyed. The remaining reticulocytes carry near-normal enzyme levels, producing a falsely reassuring result. Always test after the crisis resolves.

interactions.label: A patient's direct antiglobulin test shows C3d positivity with immunoglobulin G

params.question: A patient's direct antiglobulin test shows C3d positivity with immunoglobulin G negativity. Which condition does this pattern indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Warm AIHA is mediated by IgG antibodies that remain bound to the red cell surface at body temperature. The DAT pattern is IgG-positive, with or without C3d. An IgG-negative result argues against warm disease.

Correct. In cold AIHA, IgM antibodies bind at low temperatures and activate complement, depositing C3d on the red cell. At body temperature, the IgM dissociates, leaving only C3d detectable on the DAT.
Hereditary spherocytosis is a non-immune condition caused by intrinsic membrane protein defects. The DAT is negative — this is the key feature distinguishing it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
PNH is caused by a somatic PIG-A mutation removing complement regulators CD55 and CD59. It is diagnosed by flow cytometry detecting absent GPI-anchored proteins, not by the DAT.

overallFeedback.feedback: A DAT showing C3d positivity with IgG negativity indicates cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The IgM antibody binds in the cold periphery and activates complement, but dissociates at body temperature — so only the complement deposit (C3d) remains detectable.

C3d-only positivity on the DAT indicates cold AIHA. The IgM antibody activates complement at low temperatures but dissociates at 37°C, leaving complement fragments (C3d) as the only detectable marker on the red cell.

interactions.label: A young patient with chronic haemolytic anaemia has spherocytes on the periphera

params.question: A young patient with chronic haemolytic anaemia has spherocytes on the peripheral blood smear. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which diagnosis is most likely?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Warm AIHA also produces spherocytes via IgG-mediated partial phagocytosis, but the DAT would be positive for IgG on the red cell surface. A negative DAT argues strongly against immune-mediated spherocytosis.

Correct. Spherocytes with a negative DAT point to hereditary spherocytosis. The intrinsic membrane defect (spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3 mutations) produces spherocytes without any immune coating on the red cell.
G6PD deficiency produces bite cells (from splenic removal of Heinz bodies) due to oxidative damage, not spherocytes. The smear morphology directs you to the correct mechanism and workup.

MAHA produces schistocytes — fragmented helmet-shaped cells from mechanical shearing by fibrin strands — not spherocytes. Each morphological pattern on the smear points to a distinct pathological mechanism.

overallFeedback.feedback: The diagnostic algorithm: spherocytes on the peripheral smear trigger a DAT. Positive DAT confirms warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Negative DAT points to hereditary spherocytosis — an intrinsic membrane protein defect without immune involvement.

Spherocytes on the smear lead to the DAT. A positive DAT means warm AIHA; a negative DAT points to hereditary spherocytosis. This two-step decision is the core of the smear-based diagnostic algorithm.
